title: How do boat planks reveal connections across the sea?
essentialQuestion: How can different clues show that people were linked across the sea, and what can they not prove?
learningGoal: Combine two kinds of evidence from Butuan to make a careful claim about links across the sea, and say what the evidence cannot show.

warmUp.question: What could an old boat tell you about the people who built it?

evidence.question: Which source is about the boats, and which is about other objects? Do they have the same dates?

sources.caption: Source 1: An article by the National Museum of the Philippines, 20 September 2022
details: It says the Butuan boats are built from planks, joined with a method called lashed-lug.
It says they were built between the late 700s and the early 900s, and are the oldest boats found in the Philippines.
It says boats like these may have been built with methods shared across Southeast Asia.
Limit: the same article describes Chinese bowls found at two other places in the Philippines, Mulanay and Laurel. Those bowls were not found in Butuan.

sources.caption: Source 2: The National Museum's page about its Ginikanan/Gigikanan gallery in Butuan
details: It says the gallery shows finds dug up by treasure hunters in the 1970s.
It says these finds point to early trade with China and other parts of Southeast Asia.
Limit: the page does not give a date for each object.

sources.caption: Source 3: A National Museum article called "Bulawan", 30 September 2022
details: It says graves in the wider Butuan and Surigao area held many Chinese wares from the 900s to the 1100s.
It says some later Chinese blue-and-white wares, from the 1200s and 1300s, were found there too.
Limit: these are finds from graves. They are separate from the boats.

sources.caption: Source 4: A photo of boat planks at the Balangay Shrine Museum in Butuan, taken on 18 May 2015 by Lee
details: It shows three long, dark wooden planks on display. The nearest one has round holes along it.
Limit: it cannot show where the boat sailed, who sailed it or what it carried.

events.text: The Butuan boats are built, says the National Museum (2022).
Many of the Chinese wares later found in graves in the wider area are made.
Some later Chinese blue-and-white wares, also found in the area, are made.
Archaeologists explore the boats. Treasure hunters also dig up many other finds.
Lee photographs boat planks in a museum in Butuan.

sections.heading: A boatbuilding clue
sections.text: Butuan is a city on the island of Mindanao in the Philippines, close to rivers and the sea. In the 1970s and 1980s, archaeologists studied old wooden boats there, called balangay. The National Museum of the Philippines says the boats were built from planks, joined using a method called lashed-lug. It says they were built between the late 700s and the early 900s. The planks are maritime evidence: people here built boats for travel by water. But they do not record who sailed, what they carried or where they went. A line on a map from Butuan to another island would show a possible link, not a proven trip.
sections.simpler: Butuan is a city in the Philippines. It is near the sea. Archaeologists found old wooden boats there. These boats are called balangay. Each boat was made of long, flat pieces of wood. They were built more than 1,000 years ago. The boats are maritime evidence. They show that people built boats to travel by water. But they do not show who sailed. They do not show where the boats went.

sections.heading: A different kind of clue
sections.text: The National Museum in Butuan also shows other finds from the area. Many were dug up by treasure hunters in the 1970s. The museum says they point to early trade with China and other parts of Southeast Asia. Another museum article says graves in the wider Butuan and Surigao area held many Chinese wares, or pottery. Many were made in the 900s to 1100s, and some later. These objects were imported: made in one place and brought to another. The pottery and the boats are different finds, often from a different time and context. We can use both to ask about links across the sea. But nobody found the pottery inside a boat.
sections.simpler: The museum in Butuan has other old things too. Some came from China. They were imported. That means they were made in one place and brought to another. Chinese pottery was found in graves near Butuan. Much of it is from the 900s to the 1100s. Some is later. The pottery and the boats are different finds. Each has its own context and date. We can use both as clues. But nobody found the pottery inside a boat.

sections.heading: Test a claim
sections.text: The second picture is a photo of old balangay planks in the Balangay Shrine Museum in Butuan. It was taken in 2015, more than 1,000 years after the boats were built. Look at the shape of the wood and the round holes along it. The photo supports one claim: people in Butuan built boats from wooden planks. A bigger claim, that people in the region were linked by sea, needs more clues, such as imported objects. The photo alone cannot show the route of this boat. It also cannot tell us if trade was always fair or peaceful.
sections.simpler: The second picture is a photo of old pieces of a boat. They are in a museum in Butuan. The photo is from 2015. Can you see the holes in the wood? The photo shows that people built boats from wood. We need more clues to show links by sea. Imported things are one clue. The photo does not show where this boat went. It does not show if trade was fair.

checks.question: Can the planks in the photo prove one exact trip?

options.text: No, they show boatbuilding, not a route
options.feedback: Yes. The planks show how people built boats. A route would need other records or finds, and it might stay uncertain.

options.text: Yes, the holes show where it sailed
options.feedback: Not quite. Holes in the wood can tell us about how the boat was built, not where it went. Look at the third part of the reading.

options.text: Yes, old wood always shows a route
options.feedback: Not quite. Wood cannot record a journey. Look at what the first part of the reading says the planks do not record.

checks.question: Why should the boats and the Chinese pottery have separate dates?

options.text: The pottery was found inside the boats
options.feedback: Not quite. Nobody found the pottery inside a boat. Look at the end of the second part of the reading.

options.text: They are different finds from different times
options.feedback: Yes. They are separate finds, often from a different time and context. Each clue needs its own date.

options.text: The boats were built after the pottery
options.feedback: Not quite. The museum dates the boats to the late 700s to early 900s. Much of the pottery is from later. Check the dates in the reading.

write.prompt: Use two clues from the lesson to make a careful claim about Butuan's links across the sea. Then say one thing we cannot yet say.
sentenceStarters: Another source that could help is ...
selfCheck: I used the boats as one clue.
I used imported objects as a second clue.
I said one thing we cannot yet say.
write.example: The boat remains show that people in Butuan built wooden boats more than 1,000 years ago. The other objects suggest that people there had contact with China. Chinese pottery was found in graves nearby. These clues are different because they are separate finds. Much of the pottery is later than the boats. We cannot yet say where the boat in the photo went. Another source that could help is a record from a port across the sea.

speak.partnerTask: With a partner, answer two questions. What does the boat alone show? What extra source would help you make a claim about trade?
speak.independentTask: Say or write two sentences: one about what the boat shows, and one about a source that could support a claim about trade.

visual.description: A modern outline map, with "modern map" in one corner, of the Philippines and nearby seas: Mindanao, with a small boat symbol at Butuan on its north coast; Luzon and the Visayas in outline; Borneo, Sumatra and Java to the south-west; the Malay Peninsula and mainland Southeast Asia to the west; the coast of southern China to the north-west. Coasts are solid lines (known geography). From Butuan, three thin dashed lines run toward "China", "mainland Southeast Asia" and "Sumatra", with no arrowheads and no ships, and one shared label on the sea: "possible connections, not a documented voyage". Legend: boat symbol = "boat remains (Butuan)"; small bowl symbol beside Butuan = "imported wares found in graves in the area"; dashed line = "possible connection". A small tag beside the boat symbol only: "boats: late 700s–early 900s". A separate tag beside the bowl symbol: "wares: many 900s–1100s, some later". Do not mark Mulanay, Laurel or any other site's finds as Butuan finds.
visual.alt: A modern map of the Philippines and nearby seas. A boat symbol marks Butuan on Mindanao. Dashed lines from Butuan toward China, mainland Southeast Asia and Sumatra are labelled possible connections, not a documented voyage. Separate tags give the boats' dates and the later dates of the imported wares.
visual.caption: A modern map made for this lesson. The dashed lines show possible links, not the route of any real boat.
visual.lookClosely: Why is the connection drawn with a dashed line?

secondVisual.description: Wikimedia Commons file "Planks of a Butuan balangay in the Butuan National Museum.jpg", a photo by Lee (Flickr user lee_marq), taken on 18 May 2015 and copied to Commons from Flickr. The file's title says the Butuan National Museum, but its own description says the planks are in the Balangay Shrine Museum, so the lesson uses that. It shows three long, dark, weathered wooden planks resting on pale blue blocks, seen close up; the nearest has round holes along it. A small photographer's mark is in the bottom-left corner. Chosen because it shows real boat remains on display, so learners can ask what planks can and cannot show.
secondVisual.alt: Three long, dark, cracked wooden planks rest on pale blue blocks in a museum. The nearest plank has round holes along its length.
secondVisual.caption: Old boat planks on display at the Balangay Shrine Museum in Butuan, photographed in 2015. A photo of planks cannot show where the boat sailed.
secondVisual.lookClosely: What can you see about how the boat was built? What cannot be seen?

sensitiveNotes: Many of the imported wares come from graves, and some finds were dug up by treasure hunters. The lesson says so plainly, without detail; keep the focus on objects and dates. Exchange across the sea was not always fair or peaceful, but the lesson makes no claim either way. Never ask learners about their own or their family's journeys by sea, home countries, religion or ethnicity.
educatorNotes: Aim: learners make a two-clue claim about links across the sea and name what the evidence cannot show. Evidence move: put the boats' date (late 700s to early 900s) and the imported wares' dates (many 900s–1100s, some 1200s–1300s) in two separate boxes on the board before anyone links them. A sound answer uses two clues for wider contacts without claiming one voyage or one deposit.

Misconceptions to address: the planks in the photo are not dated to the same context as every other object, and the wares were not found in a boat. The National Museum's 2022 maritime article mentions Changsha ceramics from Mt Kamhantik in Mulanay (Quezon) and from Laurel (Batangas), not from Butuan; Butuan's own evidence is the Butuan gallery and the grave finds of the wider Agusan del Norte and Surigao del Sur area. Source caveat: published dates for the boats differ. The 2022 article gives the late 8th to early 10th centuries, while UNESCO's 2006 Tentative List entry (submitted by the National Museum) gives the 10th to 13th centuries; that difference is itself a good example of evidence being revised.
changes: Written on 1 November 2026 from Justin's course brief (28 October 2026), sections 3 and 3A.

Kept the brief's distinctions: the boats' date stands beside the boats only; the imported wares get their own dates and are described as separate grave finds from the wider Butuan and Surigao area; the 2022 maritime article's Changsha ceramics are named only as Mulanay and Laurel finds (evidence card and teacher note), never as Butuan finds.

Checked against the National Museum pages opened on 1 November 2026: the 2022 maritime article (lashed-lug boats, late 8th to early 10th centuries, oldest watercraft in the Philippines), the Boat Site Museum page (exploration in the 1970s and 1980s), the Ginikanan/Gigikanan page (finds dug up by treasure hunters in the 1970s, early trade with China and Southeast Asia) and the Bulawan article (many 10th–12th-century South China wares, some 13th–14th-century blue-and-white wares among grave goods in Agusan del Norte and Surigao del Sur). Wrote centuries as "900s to 1100s" for easier reading.

Added UNESCO's 2006 Tentative List entry as a source because it gives different dates for the boats (10th to 13th centuries); the lesson follows the newer 2022 National Museum dates and the teacher note explains the difference.

Commons file checked through the Commons API on 1 November 2026: Lee (Flickr lee_marq), taken 18 May 2015, CC BY 2.0, as the brief says; its description places the planks in the Balangay Shrine Museum. I dropped the brief caption's "This is not a modern replica": the file page says the planks are from a Butuan balangay, but I could not confirm more than that. Whether the Balangay Shrine Museum is the same place as the National Museum's Boat Site Museum in Libertad is not confirmed; a reviewer should check.
